column2: On the authority of the Commander of the Believers, Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Actions are only by intentions,

and every person shall have only what he intended. So whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated.”

Reported by the two imams of the hadith scholars, Abū ʿAbdillāh Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mughīrah ibn Bardizbah al-Bukhārī and Abū al-Ḥusayn Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj ibn Muslim al-Qushayrī al-Naysābūrī, in their two Ṣaḥīḥs, which are the most authentic of compiled books.

It was recorded by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others. ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqāṣ al-Laythī alone narrated it from ʿUmar, Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Taymī alone narrated it from him, and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī alone narrated it from the latter;

after that, many took it from him. It is therefore one of the gharīb (singly narrated) hadiths of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, and it is the book's opening hadith. Its closing hadith is like it in this respect: the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, “Two words beloved to the Most Merciful…”, which is also one of the gharīb hadiths of the Ṣaḥīḥ.

Al-Nawawī opened his Forty Hadith with this hadith, and a number of scholars have opened their books with it. Imam al-Bukhārī opened his Ṣaḥīḥ with it, ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Maqdisī his book ʿUmdat al-Aḥkām, al-Baghawī his two books Maṣābīḥ al-Sunnah and Sharḥ al-Sunnah,
and al-Suyūṭī his book al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr. At the beginning of his book al-Majmūʿ Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab, al-Nawawī devoted a section in which he said (1/35):
“Section on sincerity, truthfulness and keeping the intention present in all deeds, outward and hidden.” In it he cited three verses of the Qurʾān, then the hadith “Actions are only by intentions,”

and said: “It is an authentic hadith whose authenticity is agreed upon, and there is consensus on its great standing and importance. It is one of the principles of faith, the first of its supports and the firmest of its pillars. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This hadith enters into seventy chapters of fiqh. He also said: It is a third of knowledge.

Others said the same. It is one of the hadiths around which Islam revolves. There is disagreement over how many these are: some said three, some four, some two, and some a single hadith. I have collected them all in my Forty, and they came to forty hadiths, which no one devoted to his religion can afford not to know,

because all of them are authentic and they bring together the principles of Islam: its fundamentals and subsidiary rulings, zuhd, etiquette, noble character and other matters. I began with this hadith only in emulation of our imams and the earliest of our predecessors among the scholars (may Allah be pleased with them).

The undisputed imam of the people of hadith, Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Bukhārī, began his Ṣaḥīḥ with it, and a number of scholars have transmitted that the Salaf considered it recommended to open books with this hadith,

to alert the student to correcting his intention and to seeking the Face of Allah the Exalted in all his deeds, outward and hidden. It has been narrated to us that Imam Abū Saʿīd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
If I were to compile a book, I would begin every chapter of it with this hadith. It has also been narrated to us that he said:

Whoever wishes to compile a book, let him begin with this hadith. Imam Abū Sulaymān Ḥamd ibn Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Khaṭṭāb al-Khaṭṭābī, the Shāfiʿī imam (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him), said in his book al-Maʿālim:
Our earlier shaykhs considered it recommended to place the hadith “Actions are by intentions” at the head of everything that is begun and undertaken in matters of religion,
because every kind of them has need of it.”

Ibn Rajab said in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (1/61): “The scholars agreed on its authenticity and received it with acceptance. Al-Bukhārī placed it at the head of his book al-Ṣaḥīḥ, putting it in the place of an opening address,
as an indication from him that every deed by which the Face of Allah is not sought is void and has no fruit in this world or in the Hereafter.”

Ibn Rajab said: “This hadith is one of the hadiths around which the religion revolves. It is reported that al-Shāfiʿī said: This hadith is a third of knowledge and enters into seventy chapters of fiqh. It is reported that Imam Aḥmad said:

The foundations of Islam rest on three hadiths: the hadith of ʿUmar, ‘Actions are by intentions’; the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, ‘Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected’; and the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, ‘The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear.’”

He also said (1/71), explaining Imam Aḥmad's statement: “The whole of the religion goes back to doing what is commanded, leaving what is prohibited, and holding back from doubtful matters, and all of this is contained in the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr. But this is completed only by two things:
First, that the deed outwardly conforms to the Sunnah, and this is what the hadith of ʿĀʾishah contains: ‘Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected.’
Second, that inwardly the deed is done for the Face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as the hadith of ʿUmar contains: ‘Actions are by intentions.’”
Ibn Rajab cited statements (1/61–63) from some scholars about the hadiths around which Islam revolves: some of them said they are two, some said
four, and some said five. The hadiths he cited from them, in addition to the first three, are: “The creation of each of you is gathered in his mother's womb”;

“Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him”; “Allah is pure and accepts only what is pure”; “None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself”;

“There is to be no harm and no returning of harm”; “When I command you to do something, do of it what you are able”; “Be detached from this world and Allah will love you; be detached from what people possess and people will love you”; and “The religion is sincere counsel (naṣīḥah).”

His words, “Actions are only by intentions”: innamā (“only”) is a particle of restriction. The al- of al-aʿmāl (actions) is said by some to refer specifically to acts of devotion, and by others to be general, covering every action.

Those that are acts of devotion earn their doer a reward; and those that are matters of habit, such as eating, drinking and sleeping, also earn a reward if he intends by them to gain strength for obedience.

The al- in al-niyyāt (intentions) stands in place of the pronoun -hā (their), meaning “actions are by their intentions”. What the prepositional phrase attaches to is omitted, the implied word being “considered”, that is, actions are considered according to their intentions.

Linguistically, intention (niyyah) means aim. It serves to distinguish acts of worship from one another, such as one obligation from another or an obligation from a voluntary act, and to distinguish acts of worship from habits, such as a bath to remove major ritual impurity (janābah) from a bath taken to cool down or to get clean.

His words, “and every person shall have only what he intended”: Ibn Rajab said (1/65): “This is a statement that a person obtains from his deed only what he intended by it. If he intended good, he obtains good;

and if he intended evil, he obtains evil. This is not merely a repetition of the first sentence, for the first sentence indicated that the soundness or corruption of a deed depends on the intention that brings it about,

while the second sentence indicated that the doer's reward for his deed depends on his righteous intention, and his punishment for it on his corrupt intention. His intention may also be permissible, in which case the deed is permissible and brings him neither reward nor punishment.

So the deed in itself—its soundness, corruption or permissibility—depends on the intention that prompts it and brings it into being; and the doer's reward, punishment or freedom from both depends on the intention by which the deed became righteous, corrupt or permissible.”

His words, “So whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated.”

Hijrah (emigration) comes from hajr, which means leaving. It may be leaving a land of fear for a land of safety, like the emigration from Makkah to Abyssinia, or it may be from the lands of disbelief to the lands of Islam,

like the emigration from Makkah to Madīnah. Emigration to Madīnah came to an end with the conquest of Makkah, while emigration from the lands of shirk to the lands of Islam remains until the Hour is established.

In his words, “So whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger,” the condition and its consequence are identical, whereas normally they differ. The meaning is: whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger in intention and aim,
his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger in reward and recompense; so the two do differ. Ibn Rajab said (1/72): “When he ﷺ mentioned that deeds are according to intentions,
and that the doer's share of his deed is his intention, whether good or evil—and these are two comprehensive statements and universal principles from which nothing is excluded—

he then mentioned an example of deeds whose outward form is one, while their soundness and corruption differ according to the intentions. It is as if he were saying: all other deeds follow the pattern of this example.”
He also said (1/73): “The Prophet ﷺ informed us that this emigration differs according to the intentions and aims behind it.

Whoever emigrated to the land of Islam out of love for Allah and His Messenger, desiring to learn the religion of Islam and to practise his religion openly, which he was unable to do in the land of shirk,

he is truly the emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, and it is honour and distinction enough for him that he attained what he intended by his emigration to Allah and His Messenger. For this reason, the answer to this condition was limited to repeating its own wording,
because attaining what he intended by his emigration is the ultimate goal in this world and the Hereafter.

Whoever's emigration from the land of shirk to the land of Islam was to seek some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry in the land of Islam, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated. The first is a merchant and the second a suitor, and neither of them is an emigrant.

In his words, “to that for which he emigrated”, there is disparagement and belittling of the worldly thing he sought, since he did not mention it by name. Moreover, emigration to Allah and His Messenger is one and admits of no plurality, which is why the answer repeated the wording of the condition.

Emigration for worldly matters, however, is unlimited: a person may emigrate seeking something worldly that is permissible at one time and unlawful at another, and the particular worldly things sought by emigration are countless. That is why he said, ‘his emigration is to that for which he emigrated’, meaning whatever it may be.”
Ibn Rajab said (1/74–75): “It has become well known that the story of the man who emigrated for Umm Qays was the reason for the words of the Prophet ﷺ:

‘Whoever's emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry.’ Many later scholars mentioned this in their books, but we have not seen any basis for it with an authentic chain of narration. And Allah knows best.”
The place of the intention is the heart, and pronouncing it is an innovation. It is not permissible to pronounce the intention in any act of devotion, except in Ḥajj and ʿUmrah,

where a person may name in his talbiyah what he intends, whether qirān, ifrād or tamattuʿ, saying: “Labbayka ʿumratan wa-ḥajjan (Here I am, for ʿUmrah and Ḥajj)”, or “Labbayka ḥajjan (Here I am, for Ḥajj)”, or “Labbayka ʿumratan (Here I am, for ʿUmrah)”,
because the Sunnah is established for that and for nothing else.
There is no deed without an intention.
Deeds are judged by their intentions.
The doer's reward for his deed is according to his intention.
A scholar may give examples to clarify and explain.
Emigration is virtuous, since the Prophet ﷺ used it as his example. It is reported in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (192) from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ (may Allah be pleased with him)
that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do you not know that Islam demolishes what came before it, that emigration demolishes what came before it, and that Ḥajj demolishes what came before it?”
A person is rewarded, burdened with sin, or deprived according to his intention.

Deeds are judged by what they serve as a means to: something permissible in origin may become an act of obedience if a person intends good by it, such as eating and drinking when he intends by them to gain strength for worship.
One and the same deed may bring reward to one person and deprivation to another.
